job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Daria Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up around eight, read the job boards over tea, and send two or three applications a day. After lunch I do a practice assessment test or help my brother Yusuf with his maths homework. I graduated in July with a first in accounting and finance from Manchester, and now I'm back in my old room in Stockport. My dad Hamid drives buses and my mum Nadia is a ward nurse, and they both keep saying something will turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because the graduate market is hard enough already. At home I'd say the hype cost people two years of hiring for nothing. Online I wouldn't say much. I read more than I post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel relieved but not calm. There are plenty of openings near me, but firms like Hartley & Pryce, where I interned, take fewer graduates than they did. I think a first-year auditor now looks like a cost somebody wants to cut, and AI is just the excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Ten tailored applications a week, and the careers office on Thursdays. I'd also ask my old manager at the housing association whether a fixed-term job could open up. Nothing big changes, because I've got over six months saved and no debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, with a knot in my stomach on Sunday nights. I'm 23 with a first-class degree and I'm still at my parents' kitchen table sending applications every day. Everyone from my course either has something or is pretending to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the one pressure in your life right now that has nothing to do with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being the one with the best marks and no payslip. My mum works nights on the ward and holds the house together, and I hate that she asks whether I've heard back. Dad says it's a union issue, that firms should be made to train people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would you talk to about the job search, and what would they say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Priya, who started at a bank in Leeds, and my old tutor Dr Okafor. Priya says keep applying. Dr Okafor says my references are strong and an offer will come. It helps, but it also makes me feel I should have one already.

say: I'd say the **hype** made firms freeze graduate hiring for nothing.
I'd tell my family I'm applying every day and **something** will come.
think: Firms use **AI talk** as an excuse to hire fewer graduates, and I resent it.
I'm relieved nothing big changes, but my **first job** still isn't here.
do: Send about **ten tailored applications** a week and keep the Thursday careers appointments.
Ask my old housing association manager about a **fixed-term** role.
feel: **Steady** on the surface, with a Sunday-night knot about having no payslip yet.
S0.quote: I'm 23 with a first-class degree and I'm still at my parents' kitchen table sending applications every day.
fieldNote: Her worry is the delay to her first job, not AI itself.
Blames firms for cutting **graduate intakes**, in line with her father's union view.
Calm on the surface; the cushion lets her keep applying without panic.

steps.text: Send ten tailored applications a week to audit and finance teams
Ask the housing association manager about a fixed-term finance post

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening on the quiet. At home I'd say nobody votes on which jobs shrink, firms just stop replacing people. If my dad's union branch held a meeting on it I'd go and speak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the work I'd be hired for is the work that goes first. Reconciliations, sampling, checking spreadsheets, that was my whole internship at Hartley & Pryce. If software does that, a firm needs far fewer juniors, and I could be one of the ones who never gets taken on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen my search to the public sector, charities and housing associations, where there's still a person checking the numbers. I'd also keep applying to the big firms for the graduate schemes that remain. I'd spend savings before I'd take a job that has nothing to do with finance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, to be honest. I've done everything right, top marks, two internships, and the ground moves anyway. It makes me angry more than scared, because nobody asked us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which entry-level tasks in your field would go first, and what does that do to a job like the one you want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reconciliations, first-pass audit testing, expense checks and data entry. The firm told us in my internship that juniors learn by doing exactly those jobs, so I don't know how anyone learns if they vanish. I'd want to find the employers who still train people properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who graduated a year after you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to look for firms that publish how many trainees they take, and to ask in the interview what a graduate does in the first year. If the answer is vague, walk away. And join a union branch early, because people on their own get nowhere.

say: I'd say **nobody voted** for this and firms should answer for it.
I'd speak up at my dad's **union branch** about junior jobs.
think: The routine **checking work** I trained on is exactly what goes first.
I could be one of the people **never taken on**.
do: Widen applications to **charities, housing associations** and the public sector.
Keep applying to the **graduate schemes** that remain at big firms.
feel: **Angry** more than scared, because nobody asked graduates.
S1.quote: I've done everything right, top marks, two internships, and the ground moves anyway.
fieldNote: Expects the entry-level work she trained on to shrink, so her search could stretch.
Turns the worry into anger at employers and wants **collective** answers.
Won't use AI tools herself, which she hasn't linked to her chances yet.

steps.text: Apply to housing associations, charities and public-sector finance teams as well
Join her dad's union branch and speak at the junior jobs meeting
Keep applying for the remaining big-firm graduate schemes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest thing that has ever happened to ordinary people and it needs emergency rules. At home I'd say governments must act now, income support, limits on firing, training that actually exists. Online I'd probably finally post something angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my chosen career might be gone before it starts. Accounting is thinking work, and a thinking machine does it cheaper. I feel like I've spent four years learning a trade the week before it closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast on what I can control. I'd register for every public job scheme, ask my union-rep dad how to get a trade or care qualification in the evenings, and stop paying for anything extra. My savings would have to last, so I'd count every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Close to panic, in truth, though I'd hide it from Yusuf. It's the speed. There's no time for me to even work out what to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what changes about how you spend the next few months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The next few months become about money and a plan B. I'd stop applying only to finance and look at jobs with people in them, like healthcare administration or teaching support. I'd think about my mum's ward, because nursing is hands-on and robots come three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your family the night this was confirmed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to my mum and dad that we sit down and write down every bill, and that I'll cover what I can from my savings. I'd also tell Yusuf to carry on with school, because adults will have to sort this out. I'd cry later, on my own.

say: I'd say we need **emergency rules**: income support and limits on firing.
think: My **career** could be gone before it starts, because accounting is thinking work.
Four years of study feel like a **trade** that closes just as I finish.
do: Register for every **public job scheme** and count each month of savings.
Look into **evening courses** in care or healthcare administration.
feel: Near **panic**, though I'd hide it from my younger brother.
S2.quote: I feel like I've spent four years learning a trade the week before it closes.
fieldNote: Expects her **whole field** to vanish, so the cushion matters but doesn't calm her.
Her answer turns to the family: parents' bills and protecting her brother.
Looks to hands-on work and public support, consistent with her **left-leaning** views.

steps.text: Register for every public job scheme and training offer
Write down every household bill and cut extras for the family
Start an evening course in healthcare administration
Join her dad's union campaign for emergency rules on firing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to make rules if governments start tomorrow. I'd bring it up at every opportunity at my dad's union branch. Friends would say I'm being dramatic, but the ones in finance would privately agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my first job might be my only one in finance, and it won't last. I'd still get a job in the meantime, because there are plenty of openings now. I think the first three years would be fine and then it gets hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take the best job I can get, learn everything, and save hard. I'd put half of every salary away and start an evening course in something with people in it, maybe project coordination. I'd also join the union at work on the first day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a slower kind. There's time to plan, but I'm not sure I'll use it well. I tend to wait for things to be proven before I change anything, which is a habit I'd have to fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years of warning, what would you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm in survival mode. With five, I'd actually take a job and build a cushion, and I'd choose a firm that talks honestly about what's coming. I'd avoid a long fixed-rate mortgage, which I'd otherwise plan on at 27.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd stop doing, or start doing, that you wouldn't if it were sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop assuming a 40-year career in audit. I'd start thinking of finance as the first chapter. And I'd put effort into getting to know the people who will run things, because relationships will matter more than a certificate.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **make rules** if governments start now.
I'd **join the union** on my first day at work.
think: My first finance job may be my only one, and it **won't last**.
I'd probably wait too long to change, which is a **habit** I'd fight.
do: Take the **best job** I can get and save half of every salary.
Start an **evening course** in project coordination.
feel: A slower **anxiety**: time to plan, but doubt that I'd use it well.
S3.quote: I'd stop assuming a 40-year career in audit. I'd start thinking of finance as the first chapter.
fieldNote: More time lets her **earn and save** before the shock instead of scrambling.
Admits her resistant streak, waiting for proof, could cost her.

steps.text: Take the best finance job offered and learn everything there
Save half of each salary for five years
Take an evening course in project coordination

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and we should use it to rebuild how the whole system works. At home I'd say hold the politicians to it. I'd probably vote differently and push my local union to demand training funds now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think ten years gives me a full career's start. I'd have a decade of earning, and I'd learn to work alongside whatever comes. I'd still worry for my brother, because he'll be 25 when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first good offer, build up my skills at that firm, and finish a professional accounting qualification. If it's still worth anything by 2036, great. If not, I'd have had ten years of income to move on with, and I'd start learning one small AI tool a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly okay, to be honest. I'd have time to find my feet. A bit guilty too, because people my parents' age won't have that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put in the time on the accounting qualification and tell myself it's a bridge and not a destination. I'd also spend a year trying one AI tool at work, even though I don't like them. If a firm proved it was worth it I'd stop resisting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having a decade make you feel safe, or does it just push the worry further off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer than two years, much safer, but not safe. The decade lets the worry go quiet, then a headline wakes it up. I'd probably feel it every time a firm announced it was replacing a team.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long runway** and we should use it to rebuild the system.
I'd push my local **union** to demand training funds now.
think: Ten years gives me a **real start** to my career.
I worry more for my brother, who will be **25** when it lands.
do: Take the first good offer and finish a **professional accounting** qualification.

feel: Fairly **okay**, with some guilt for people whose parents' generation won't get this time.
S4.quote: The decade lets the worry go quiet, then a headline wakes it up.
fieldNote: Time turns her **resistance** into slow, grudging openness to AI tools.

steps.text: Finish a professional accounting qualification while working

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, by a mile. There's nothing I could do in time, and I'd have to watch my parents worry about money. What would help is income support that doesn't take months to arrive, real training that leads somewhere, and firms being made to keep hiring trainees. I'd also want a plain, honest explanation from government, not slogans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not as sure of myself as I sound. I look like the person who'll be fine, with a first-class degree and savings. But I haven't had a job yet. Every month it's quieter in my head. I'd like to be asked how it feels to be the one everyone expects to do well.

headlineQuote: I look like the person who'll be fine, with a first-class degree and savings. But I haven't had a job yet.
portrait: Daria is 23, a **top graduate** in accounting and finance from Manchester, living in her parents' Stockport home.
Her dad, a bus driver and union rep, shapes her view that **employers** must train people.
She never uses AI tools and prefers the familiar, which makes her slow to adapt.
Mood moves from **uneasy** with no shock to alarmed in the two-year world, where she fears her field vanishes.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because she would have no time to find a new path.
whatWouldHelp: **Fast income support**, real training that leads to work, and firms made to keep hiring trainees.
